questions.question: What is the difference between 'var', 'let', and 'const'? What is hoisting?
options: They are identical; hoisting means variables are moved to the bottom
var is function-scoped and hoisted (initialized as undefined); let/const are block-scoped with TDZ. const cannot be reassigned
let is global-scoped, const is block-scoped, var is file-scoped
const makes values completely immutable including nested object properties
questions.explanation: var is function-scoped and HOISTED (initialized as undefined before code runs). let and const are BLOCK-scoped and have a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) — accessing them before declaration throws ReferenceError. const prevents REASSIGNMENT of the binding but does NOT freeze objects — their properties can still change.

questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript? Give a real-world use case.
options: A closure is a way to close/terminate a function's execution
A closure is when a function retains access to variables from its outer scope even after that scope has finished executing
A closure only works with arrow functions, not regular functions
A closure is the same as a class in JavaScript
questions.explanation: A closure is a function that 'remembers' the environment where it was created. Every time you create a function inside another function, the inner function has access to the outer function's variables — even after the outer function returns. This is fundamental for data privacy, memoization, and event handlers.

questions.question: What is event bubbling and event delegation? How do you stop bubbling?
options: Event bubbling is when an event fires from parent to child. stopPropagation() prevents it
Event bubbling is when an event fires on an element and propagates UP to parent elements. Event delegation uses this to handle multiple children with ONE listener on the parent
Event delegation means adding individual event listeners to each child element
stopPropagation() and preventDefault() do the same thing
questions.explanation: Event Bubbling: when you click a button inside a div, the click event fires on the button FIRST, then 'bubbles up' to div, then body, then document. Event Delegation exploits this: instead of adding 100 listeners to 100 items, add ONE listener to the parent and check event.target. e.stopPropagation() stops the bubble. e.preventDefault() stops the browser's default behavior (like form submit).

questions.question: Explain destructuring in JavaScript. What are the advanced use cases?
options: Destructuring only works with arrays, not objects
Destructuring extracts values from arrays/objects into variables. Advanced: renaming, defaults, rest, nested, function params
Destructuring creates a deep copy of the object
Destructuring only works with ES5 syntax
questions.explanation: Destructuring is syntactic sugar for extracting values from objects/arrays. It's EVERYWHERE in React: const { data, loading } = useQuery(); const [state, setState] = useState(). Master all forms — you'll use them daily.

questions.question: What is currying in functional programming? How does it differ from partial application?
options: Currying is a type of recursion for processing arrays
Currying transforms a function with multiple args into a sequence of single-arg functions. Partial application fixes some args and returns a function waiting for the rest
Currying and partial application are identical concepts with different names
Currying only works with pure functions that return primitives
questions.explanation: Currying: f(a, b, c) → f(a)(b)(c). Each call returns a new function waiting for the next arg. Partial Application: fix SOME args, return function for the remaining. Both enable function composition and reusability — foundational to functional programming.

questions.question: Explain the difference between async/await and Promises. What happens with error handling?
options: async/await replaces Promises entirely and is always faster
async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises. async functions always return Promises. await pauses execution within the async function. Use try/catch for errors vs .catch()
async/await cannot be used with Promise.all()
await blocks the entire JavaScript thread (synchronous)
questions.explanation: async/await makes asynchronous code READ like synchronous code. async functions ALWAYS return a Promise (even if you return a primitive). await pauses ONLY within the async function, not the whole app — the event loop continues. Errors: use try/catch with await, or .catch() with Promise chains.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'interface' and 'type' in TypeScript? When to use each?
options: They are completely identical; use either one

interface is for object shapes and is extendable/mergeable via declaration merging. type is more flexible: unions, intersections, primitives, tuples. Prefer interface for objects, type for complex types
type is deprecated, always use interface
interface supports generics but type does not
questions.explanation: Both define shapes, but differ in key ways: Interface supports declaration merging (defining it twice merges them), is better for public API contracts. Type supports unions (A | B), intersections (A & B), mapped types, conditional types. Rule of thumb: interface for object shapes/classes, type for everything else.

questions.question: What are TypeScript Generics and why are they essential for reusable code?
options: Generics are only used in class components, not functional ones
Generics create reusable components/functions that work with ANY type while preserving type safety. <T> is a type placeholder filled at call time
Generics replace the 'any' type and always slow down compilation
Generics are a runtime feature of TypeScript that adds overhead
questions.explanation: Generics are like type-safe templates. Instead of using 'any' (which removes type safety), Generics let you say 'this works with ANY type, and TypeScript will figure it out from context'. Essential for hooks, API wrappers, utility functions, and component libraries.

questions.question: What are TypeScript Utility Types? Name and explain at least 4 essential ones.
options: Utility Types are just type aliases with different names
Utility Types are built-in type transformers: Partial<T> (all optional), Required<T> (all required), Pick<T, K> (select keys), Omit<T, K> (exclude keys), Record<K, V>, Readonly<T>
Utility Types only work with interfaces, not type aliases
Utility Types are deprecated in TypeScript 5+
questions.explanation: Utility Types save you from rewriting type transformations. They are built into TypeScript and essential for real-world apps. Mastering them shows TypeScript fluency in interviews.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'unknown' and 'any' in TypeScript? Which is safer and why?
options: They are identical, both disable type checking
'any' disables all type checking (escape hatch). 'unknown' is type-safe: you MUST narrow the type before using it. Always prefer 'unknown' over 'any'
'unknown' is the old name for 'any' in TypeScript 3
'unknown' can only hold primitive values, 'any' holds objects too
questions.explanation: 'any' tells TypeScript: 'trust me, I know what this is' — TypeScript stops checking. It's a red flag in code reviews. 'unknown' says: 'I don't know the type yet' — TypeScript forces you to CHECK before using it. Type narrowing (typeof, instanceof, type guards) is needed to work with 'unknown'.

questions.question: In Next.js, what is the difference between SSR, SSG, ISR, and CSR? When do you use each?
options: They are all the same rendering strategy, just different names

SSR: renders on every request (fresh data). SSG: renders at build time (static, fastest). ISR: SSG + revalidation interval. CSR: renders in browser (SEO bad but interactive). Choose based on data freshness needs
SSG always requires a database connection at build time
CSR is always faster than SSR because it skips the server
questions.explanation: Rendering strategy is one of the most important decisions in Next.js. SSR: always fresh, good for personalized/dynamic content. SSG: lightning fast, pre-built HTML, great for blogs/landing pages. ISR: best of both — static but refreshes every N seconds. CSR: data fetches in the browser, no server needed but bad for SEO.

questions.question: Explain the difference between useEffect, useLayoutEffect, and useInsertionEffect in React.
options: They are all identical; use useEffect for everything
useEffect: after paint (async). useLayoutEffect: after DOM mutations but BEFORE paint (blocks paint). useInsertionEffect: before DOM mutations (for CSS-in-JS libraries)
useLayoutEffect is deprecated in React 18
useInsertionEffect is the same as useEffect with an empty dependency array
questions.explanation: The ORDER of execution: 1) DOM mutations happen, 2) useInsertionEffect fires (inject styles), 3) useLayoutEffect fires (read/modify DOM synchronously), 4) Browser paints, 5) useEffect fires (side effects). Use useLayoutEffect when you need to measure DOM or prevent visual flicker. Use useEffect for 99% of cases.

questions.question: What are React Server Components (RSC) in Next.js 14? How are they different from Client Components?
options: Server Components are just components rendered with getServerSideProps

Server Components render ONLY on the server — zero JS sent to client. Client Components ('use client') can use hooks and browser APIs. RSC enables streaming, reduces bundle size, and allows direct DB access
Server Components require a special export format unlike regular components
Server Components and Client Components cannot be used in the same tree
questions.explanation: React Server Components is the biggest shift in React since hooks. Server Components: run ONLY on server, zero bundle size, can access DB/filesystem directly, CAN'T use useState/useEffect/browser APIs. Client Components ('use client'): run on server AND client, CAN use hooks. You CAN mix them — Server Components can render Client Components as children.

questions.question: Explain all 5 SOLID principles with a React/TypeScript example for each.
options: SOLID stands for: Simple, Ordered, Loose, Interactive, Dynamic

S: Single Responsibility (one reason to change). O: Open/Closed (extend not modify). L: Liskov Substitution (subtypes replaceable). I: Interface Segregation (small interfaces). D: Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions)
SOLID only applies to backend code. Frontend only needs DRY
The 'L' in SOLID stands for Lazy loading
questions.explanation: SOLID is the foundation of maintainable OOP and functional code. Every experienced developer should know these by heart. In interviews, expect to explain at least 2-3 with concrete examples from your actual work.

questions.question: What is Clean Architecture in a React/Next.js project? How do you structure folders?
options: Clean Architecture means having a /components folder
Clean Architecture separates concerns into layers: Domain (entities, business logic) → Application (use cases, hooks) → Infrastructure (API, storage) → Presentation (UI). Dependencies point inward
Clean Architecture requires using Redux as the state manager
Clean Architecture is only for enterprise apps, not startups
questions.explanation: Clean Architecture's core rule: THE DEPENDENCY RULE — source code dependencies must point INWARD. The domain layer knows nothing about React, the API, or the database. This makes the business logic independently testable and the implementation details swappable.

questions.question: You improved app performance by 30% at Omnitrek. What specific techniques did you use? (Lazy loading, CDN, Code splitting)
options: Just minifying CSS files reduces performance by 30%

Lazy loading: load components/images only when needed (React.lazy, Suspense, dynamic()). Code splitting: split bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand. CDN: serve static assets from edge locations closer to users
Code splitting and lazy loading are the same technique
CDN only helps with video files, not JavaScript or images
questions.explanation: This is YOUR real experience from Omnitrek! These three techniques together compound beautifully: Code Splitting reduces initial bundle size. Lazy Loading defers loading until needed. CDN reduces latency for asset delivery. Next.js does code splitting automatically per page, and dynamic() adds component-level splitting.

questions.question: What are CSS BEM, SMACSS, and OOCSS? When would you use each methodology?
options: They are all CSS frameworks like Bootstrap or Tailwind
BEM: Block__Element--Modifier naming convention for CSS scalability. SMACSS: categorizes styles (base, layout, module, state, theme). OOCSS: separates structure from skin for reusability
BEM is a JavaScript framework, not a CSS methodology
These are outdated; Tailwind CSS completely replaces all three
questions.explanation: CSS Architectures prevent the 'specificity war' and naming collision hell in large apps. BEM is the most widely used: .block__element--modifier makes the relationship explicit. In React projects, CSS Modules or Tailwind solve similar problems, but understanding BEM shows architectural thinking.

questions.question: What is the difference between unit tests, integration tests, and E2E tests? What tools do you use for each?
options: All tests are the same; the tool used defines the type

Unit: tests single function/component in isolation (Jest/Vitest). Integration: tests multiple units working together (React Testing Library). E2E: tests full user flows in real browser (Cypress/Playwright)
Integration tests are just slower unit tests
E2E tests replace unit tests in modern development
questions.explanation: The Testing Pyramid: many unit tests (fast, cheap) → fewer integration tests → even fewer E2E tests (slow, expensive). React Testing Library philosophy: 'test behavior, not implementation'. From your resume: you have Vitest + React Testing Library certifications — mention this!

questions.question: What is mocking in tests and why is it essential? How do you mock in Jest/Vitest?
options: Mocking means creating fake UI designs to test with
Mocking replaces real implementations (API calls, modules, functions) with controlled fakes during tests. Essential for: isolation, speed, avoiding external dependencies, testing error states
Mocking only works with class-based components
You should never mock — always use real implementations in tests
questions.explanation: Mocking is what makes tests FAST and RELIABLE. Without mocks: your unit tests make real HTTP requests (slow, flaky, depends on network). With mocks: tests run in milliseconds, always return predictable data, and can simulate errors. vi.fn() / jest.fn() creates a spy that tracks calls.

questions.question: How would you introduce yourself in English using your ~4 years of experience at Omnitrek? Structure your answer.
options: Just list your skills without context
Use Present-Past-Future: Current role/skills (30s) → Key achievements at Omnitrek with numbers (45s) → Why this role excites you (30s). Lead with impact.
Recite your resume from the beginning chronologically
Mention your personal life and hobbies first to seem approachable
questions.explanation: Present-Past-Future with numbers makes you memorable. Your real achievements: 30% performance improvement, 20% team efficiency with Storybook, zero-downtime CI/CD. Mention your AI-native workflow with Cursor — it's a differentiator that senior devs appreciate.

questions.question: How do you explain the Storybook implementation that improved team efficiency by 20%? Use the STAR method.
options: Just say 'I implemented Storybook' without context

STAR: Situation (team lacking component documentation) → Task (your responsibility) → Action (set up Storybook, wrote stories, created guidelines) → Result (20% efficiency improvement, specific metrics)
Downplay it because 20% might seem small
Only mention the technical implementation, skip the business impact
questions.explanation: This is gold in your resume — a real, quantified achievement. Interviewers LOVE specific numbers. Don't just say 'I used Storybook' — explain the BEFORE (problem), the WHY you chose Storybook, the WHAT you built, and the RESULT with metrics.
questions.codeExample:
// YOUR STORYBOOK STAR STORY
// (Customize with actual details from your experience)

// SITUATION:
'Our React application at Omnitrek had over 50 UI components
but no visual documentation. New developers spent significant
time understanding existing components before they could
contribute, and designers had difficulty seeing all component
states without running the full app.'

// TASK:

// ACTION:

I wrote stories for all existing components covering multiple

// RESULT:
'This resulted in a 20% improvement in team development efficiency,
measured through our sprint velocity metrics. New developers could
onboard to the component library in hours instead of days, and
design reviews dropped from 2 rounds to 1 on average.'

questions.question: What is WAI-ARIA and why is it important? What are the key ARIA attributes you should know?
options: WAI-ARIA is a CSS framework for creating accessible color schemes

WAI-ARIA is a specification that adds semantic meaning to HTML for screen readers and assistive technologies. Key attributes: role, aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-hidden, aria-live
WAI-ARIA only matters for government websites
WAI-ARIA replaces semantic HTML elements like <nav> and <button>
questions.explanation: Accessibility is NOT optional — it's in your skills evaluation (mandatory: WAI-ARIA). ARIA fills gaps when HTML semantics aren't enough. Rule: first use semantic HTML (<button>, <nav>, <main>). Add ARIA only when HTML isn't sufficient. ARIA on wrong elements can WORSEN accessibility.

questions.question: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and Cookies? When do you use each?
options: They all store data the same way, just with different capacities

localStorage: persists until manually cleared (~5-10MB). sessionStorage: cleared when tab closes. Cookies: sent with EVERY HTTP request, can be HTTP-only (XSS safe), have expiry dates. Use cookies for auth tokens, localStorage for user preferences
Cookies are insecure and should never be used for authentication
sessionStorage persists between browser restarts
questions.explanation: These are in your skills evaluation (mandatory). Key insight: localStorage and sessionStorage are client-side only (vulnerable to XSS). Cookies with HttpOnly=true are NOT accessible via JavaScript — making them the SECURE choice for auth tokens. Never store tokens in localStorage!

questions.question: What is Storybook and how does it implement component-driven development? (From your Omnitrek experience)
options: Storybook is a testing framework like Jest for snapshot testing

Storybook is a UI workshop: isolated component development with interactive documentation. Each 'story' shows a component state. Enables design-dev collaboration, visual regression testing, and auto-documentation
Storybook requires Redux to manage component state
Storybook only works with class-based React components
questions.explanation: This is YOUR real experience! Storybook implements the Component Story Format (CSF). Each story = one component state. Decorators wrap stories with providers (ThemeProvider, Router). Addons enable: controls (interactive props), actions (event tracking), accessibility audit, viewport testing.
